idiom_name: compaction pass + tail release (partition, then shorten)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form of the decision, in two steps that must always be paired. First a single forward pass with two cursors - a read cursor over the range and a write cursor starting at the first element to consider - moves every element the predicate retains down to the write position; the pass visits each element exactly once, keeps the survivors' relative order, and returns the position of the new logical end without touching the stored size or the storage. Second, the release step asks the owning container (or the separate length variable, when storage and length live apart as in C) to shorten itself to that position: a range erase/truncate/destroy where the container can do it, a size assignment plus zeroing of the dead tail where it cannot. Choose a library form of the same two steps whenever the language has one (std::erase_if, List<T>.RemoveAll, MutableList.removeAll, Vec::retain, removeAll(where:), slices.DeleteFunc); write the pass out only when the storage model offers no library path, when the predicate must also inspect or mutate the tail, or when the removed elements have to be harvested rather than dropped. Copying into a fresh sequence is a different trade - one allocation, identity lost - and should be named as such instead of passing for this idiom.
pitfalls: Stopping after the compaction: without the release step the removed elements are still in the sequence and its size is unchanged.
Compacting a container whose erase is per node (list, map) or whose storage is shared - the pass costs a full scan for nothing, or mutates data other readers are using.
Leaving the removed tail uninitialised after a manual pass: stale pointers (double free, use after free) and readable copies of values that were supposed to be gone.
